quality.question: My grey text on a white background looks faint, is that a problem?
quality.answer:
Yes — faint grey text on white can be a problem if it’s considered non-text content or text acting like a graphic, because non-text visual information must meet 3:1 contrast against its background under Level AA Success Criterion 1.4.11. [1][3]

If the grey marks are text presented as normal text, they fall under other contrast rules (see 1.4.3/1.4.11 relationship) and heavily stylized or symbolic characters may be treated as non-text for 1.4.11, so ensure meaningful visual cues achieve at least 3:1 contrast or provide an alternative high-contrast visual cue (for example additional text or an equivalent component). [3][1][2]

Also note focus indicators are required to meet 1.4.11 contrast when they identify component state, so low-contrast focus outlines on white would also fail 1.4.11 even if the component appearance is otherwise exempt. [5][1]

quality.question: buttons too small?
quality.answer: Level AA — SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum): Buttons that are too small must either meet the minimum target size (24 by 24 CSS pixels) or have sufficient spacing so adjacent targets are not too close; otherwise the success criterion is not met [2][4][5]. Users with dexterity or fine-motor difficulties (hand tremors, spasticity, etc.) benefit from the minimum size or spacing to avoid accidental activation [1][2]. Technique example: you can use CSS (min-width/min-height) to ensure sufficient spacing or size, but techniques are examples, not the only way to comply [3].

quality.question: What contrast do large text and icons need?
quality.answer:
Level AA (Success Criterion 1.4.3): Large-scale (large) text and images of large-scale text must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 [2][4].  
Level AAA (Success Criterion 1.4.6): Large-scale text and images of large-scale text must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 [1][3].

(Icons: treated as images of text or graphical objects — large icons used as text/meaningful visuals follow the same large-scale contrast requirements above) [5].

quality.question: What's the difference between 1.4.3 and 1.4.6?
quality.answer:
Level AA (1.4.3): requires text and images of text to have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (with exceptions for large-scale text at 3:1, incidental text, inactive UI components, pure decoration, text not visible to anyone, pictures with significant other visual content, and logotypes) [1].  
Level AAA (1.4.6): requires a higher contrast ratio for text and images of text — at least 7:1 (with exceptions for large-scale text at 4.5:1, incidental text, inactive UI components, pure decoration, text not visible to anyone, pictures with significant other visual content, and logotypes) [2].

quality.question: Does disabled button text need good contrast?
quality.answer:
Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Contrast (Minimum)): Text that is part of an inactive user interface component (for example, disabled button text) has no contrast requirement. [2]

Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast): Visual information required to identify user interface components and states must have at least 3:1 contrast, except for inactive components. Thus inactive (disabled) components are exempt from the 1.4.11 requirement. [1]

quality.question: Does a logo need to meet contrast rules?
quality.answer:
Level AA (SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast): Text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement; logos are exempt from the non-text contrast requirement. [2][4]

(Level AA for text contrast SC 1.4.3 is also explicit that logotypes have no contrast requirement.) [2]

quality.question: Which success criteria are new in WCAG 2.2?
quality.answer: The following success criteria are new in WCAG 2.2: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (AA), 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) (AAA), 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA), 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA), 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A), 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A), 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (AA), and 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (AAA) [2].

quality.question: At what width must content reflow without horizontal scrolling?
quality.answer: Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Reflow): content must reflow without horizontal scrolling at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels (i.e., test at 1280 CSS pixels viewport wide with 400% zoom) [2][1].

quality.question: How many times per second can content flash?
quality.answer:
Level AA (SC 2.3.1): Content must not include flashing that exceeds the specified flash thresholds (i.e., avoid flashes likely to cause seizures) — effectively you must ensure content does not produce hazardous flash patterns [2][3].  
Level AAA (SC 2.3.2): Content must not flash more than three times in any 1‑second period (no more than 3 flashes per second) [4][5][3].

quality.question: Can I use a puzzle CAPTCHA on my login page?
quality.answer:
Level AA (3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)): You may use an object-recognition CAPTCHA (including recognizing pictures the website provided) as part of authentication because such object-recognition tests are excepted at Level AA, but any CAPTCHA that is a cognitive function test (e.g., requiring remembering/transcribing a word or other cognitive tasks beyond the allowed exceptions) is not permitted unless it fits the exception. [5]

Level AAA (3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)): You may NOT use CAPTCHAs that display selections of images, videos, or audio clips where users must choose images containing a specific object (for example a puzzle requiring identifying objects) as a required step of authentication; these object-recognition approaches are not excepted at AAA. [4][5]
